tin9-bai-toan-tin-hoc.tag: Reading Steps to solve a computing problem
tin9-bai-toan-tin-hoc.reading:
Read part 2 (textbook pages 80–81). Solving a computing problem follows steps like the problem-solving process in Lesson 14. To calculate wages with a computer:
  • 1) Define the problem: find the input and the output. The input is the hourly wage (muc_luong) and the working hours (tgian_laodong). The output is the wage (tien_luong).
  • 2) Design the algorithm: split the problem into smaller problems by answering: (1) Which steps do we need? (2) In which order? First, the problem can be split into three steps in sequence: Step 1. Input the data: muc_luong and tgian_laodong. Step 2. Process the data to calculate tien_luong. Step 3. Output tien_luong. Keep splitting until each step can become a computer command. Describe the algorithm with only the basic control structures (sequence, branching and loop), as in Figure 15.3.

q4.label: Reading – Steps to solve a computing problem
q4.q: Put the steps to solve a computing problem in the correct order.
q4.k: Define the problem → Design the algorithm → Implement the algorithm → Debug and improve the program.

q4m.label: Reading – The steps for the wage problem
q4m.q: Which step of solving the wage problem is each job?
q4m.k: 1 – Define the problem; 2 – Design the algorithm; 3 – Implement the algorithm; 4 – Debug and improve.
items: The input is muc_luong, tgian_laodong; the output is tien_luong.
Split into: input the data, calculate the wage, output the result; draw the flowchart in Figure 15.3.
Write a program for the algorithm, with extra variables luong_dmuc, luong_vuot.
Run the program with different data and fix errors so it works correctly.

tin9-danh-gia-chat-luong-thong-tin.reading:
You can find information in many places, but information on the Internet is not equally reliable. For each need, think about which source has the authority:
  • Information about grade 10 admissions is on the website of the Department of Education and Training (usually edu.vn, for example phutho.edu.vn, Figure 3.3).
  • Information about school activities and clubs is on the school website.
  • Not all information is on those websites. Compare and check information before you use it.

ng.label: Task 1 – Where to look?
ng.q: Where should you look for each kind of information so it is reliable?
ng.k: 1 – a, 2 – b, 3 – c, 4 – d. For each need, look for a source with authority. Information from AI or the Internet in general must be compared and checked before you use it.
items: 1) Grade 10 admission information
2) The school's activities and clubs
3) A list of high schools near your home
4) The school's awards in competitions and Olympiads
opts: a) The website of the Department of Education and Training
c) An AI chatbot, then check the answer
d) A search engine, using official newspapers first

dm.label: Task 1 – Domain names
dm.q: What domain do the websites of Departments of Education and Training usually have?
dm.k: They usually end in edu.vn, for example phutho.edu.vn (Figure 3.3).

ai.label: Task 1 – Using AI
ai.q: You ask an AI chatbot “Name the high schools near Vinh Tuong, Phu Tho” and get a table of results (Figure 3.2). What should you do?
ai.k: AI helps you narrow the search quickly, but the answer may be wrong or old. Compare and check it with an official source before you use it.
o: Use it at once because AI is always right.
Do not use it because AI is always wrong.
Use it to narrow the search, then check with the websites of the Department of Education and the schools.
Use it only if the table has many schools.

tin9-giai-quyet-van-de.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 76–77). In Activity 1, the robot moved so that the wall was always on its right. In this way the wall leads the robot through the maze until it finds the Exit. Finding the Exit is a problem, solved in these steps:
  • Understand the problem: find what is given and what we need. The robot must find the Exit with no one to ask and no map. At each place it must choose a direction (turn right, go straight or turn left).
  • Analyse the problem: split it into smaller, easier problems. The robot's decision has three cases: turn right, go straight, turn left. With no map, the robot can only use the position of the wall.
  • Choose a solution: choose a way to solve the problem and describe it clearly. To keep the wall on the right, the robot chooses directions from right to left (Figure 14.2): a) If there is no wall on the right, turn right. b) If there is a wall on the right but not in front, go straight. c) If there are walls on the right and in front, turn left and choose again.

b14.label: Reading – The steps of problem solving
b14.q: In Activity 1, which step of problem solving is each job?
b14.k: 1 – Understand the problem; 2 – Analyse the problem; 3 – Choose a solution; 4 – Carry out the solution; 5 – Evaluate the result.
items: Find out: we need the Exit, the robot has no one to ask and no map.
Split the choice of direction into three cases: turn right, go straight, turn left.
Choose the rule “from right to left” to always keep the wall on the right.
The robot moves in the chosen way, like running an algorithm.
Test the robot in many different mazes to improve it.

tt.label: Reading – Three situations (Figure 14.2)
tt.q: Match each situation with the robot's choice in the right-wall algorithm.
tt.k: a) turn right; b) go straight; c) turn left and choose again.
items: a) No wall on the right
b) A wall on the right, no wall in front
c) Walls on the right and in front
opts: Turn right (turn right, then one step forward)
Turn left and choose the direction again

b5.label: Reading – The order of the steps
b5.q: Put the steps of problem solving in the correct order.
b5.k: Understand the problem → Analyse the problem → Choose a solution → Carry out the solution → Evaluate the result.

vd.q: Match each request with its formula (try it in the spreadsheet simulation).

thamso.label: Reading – COUNTIF arguments
thamso.q: In the formula =COUNTIF(range, criteria), match each argument with its meaning.

items: range
criteria

b) The condition to check the cells in range

g2.label: Reading – The formula in cell G2
g2.q: Why is =COUNTIF($B$3:$B$10,"Ở") in cell G2 changed to =COUNTIF($B$3:$B$10,F2)?
g2.k: Using cell F2 (a relative address) as the condition lets you copy the formula for the other spending items; the range $B$3:$B$10 (an absolute address) stays the same.

Because the old formula gave a wrong result.

tin9-ham-if.reading: Read part 1 (textbook page 49). Using the 50-30-20 budgeting rule, you can comment on each spending group. For Needs: If the spending rate is greater than 50%, the comment is “More”, otherwise it is “Less”. To write the comments in cells O3 to O5 (Figure 12a.3), use the IF function: =IF(logical_test,[value_if_true],[value_if_false]). logical_test: the condition to check; value_if_true: the value returned if the condition is true; value_if_false: the value returned if the condition is false. In Figure 12a.3 the rate for Needs is in cell N3, so the formula in cell O3 is =IF(N3>50%,"Nhiều hơn","Ít hơn") (“More”, “Less”).

ts.label: Reading – IF arguments
ts.q: In the formula =IF(logical_test,[value_if_true],[value_if_false]), match each argument with its meaning.
ts.k: logical_test – a; value_if_true – b; value_if_false – c.
items: logical_test
value_if_true
value_if_false
opts: b) The value returned if the condition is true
c) The value returned if the condition is false

o3.label: Reading – The formula in cell O3
o3.q: Cell N3 is 90.5%. The formula =IF(N3>50%,"Nhiều hơn","Ít hơn") in cell O3 gives:
o3.k: 90.5% > 50% is true → it returns value_if_true: “Nhiều hơn” (More).

tin9-ham-sumif.reading: Read part 1 (textbook pages 45–46). To manage a family budget, you need the total money for each income and spending item, so you can balance them. For example, you can avoid spending too much on things you do not need. To add up the money for each item, use SUMIF: =SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]). range: the cells to check, or to add up if there is no sum_range; criteria: the condition; sum_range (optional): the cells to add up; if it is left out, the cells in range that meet the condition are added. Table 11a.1 shows the two ways to use SUMIF.

b111.label: Reading – Table 11a.1
b111.q: Match each formula with its meaning (try it in the spreadsheet simulation).
b111.k: Form 1 (no sum_range): add the cells in range that meet the condition. Form 2: check range A2:A5 and add the matching cells in sum_range B2:B5.
items: =SUMIF(A2:A5,"Khoa",B2:B5)
opts: a) Add the values greater than 5 in A1:A5
b) Add the values in B2:B5 where the matching cell in A2:A5 is “Khoa” (the total Khoa spent)

thamso.label: Reading – SUMIF arguments
thamso.q: In the formula =SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]), match each argument with its meaning.
thamso.k: range – a; criteria – b; sum_range – c.
items: range
criteria
sum_range (optional)
opts: a) The cells to check, or to add up if there is no sum_range
c) The cells to add up; if left out, add the cells in range that meet the condition

chon.label: Reading – Choose the right function
chon.q: Which function should you use for each question about the Spending worksheet?
chon.k: Total of a whole range: SUM. Count with a condition: COUNTIF. Add with a condition: SUMIF (for example =SUMIF(D3:D10,">1000")).
items: The total of all spending
How many times was money spent on “Ở” (housing)?
The total money spent on “Ở” (housing)
How many payments were over 1 000 thousand dong?
The total of the payments over 1 000 thousand dong

h2.label: Reading – The formula in cell H2
h2.q: Which formula in cell H2 (Figure 11a.2) can be copied correctly to H3…H10?
h2.k: The item name “Ở” is in cell F2, so the condition is F2 (it changes when copied); both ranges must be absolute addresses: =SUMIF($B$3:$B$10,F2,$D$3:$D$10).

tin9-khai-thac-phan-mem-mo-phong.tag: Practice a), b) Open the software and build a circuit
tin9-khai-thac-phan-mem-mo-phong.reading:
• Like Task 1, choose SIMULATIONS → Physics → Circuit Construction Kit: DC – Virtual Lab.
  • Drag the Battery, Light Bulb, Ammeter, Switch and Wire icons to the work area and connect the parts of the circuit (Figure 6.5a).
  • Note: connect the ammeter in series with the part you measure, and never connect it directly to the two ends of the battery (Figure 6.5b).

am1.label: Task 2 – Measuring device
am1.q: Which device do you use to measure the current in a circuit?
am1.k: Use an ammeter to measure current (unit: ampere, A). A voltmeter measures voltage.

am2.label: Task 2 – How to connect
am2.q: Is the ammeter connected in parallel or in series with the part you measure?
am2.k: The ammeter is connected in series, so the current through the part also goes through the ammeter (Figure 6.5a).
o: Directly to the two ends of the battery.

am3.label: Task 2 – A problem
am3.q: In Figure 6.5b the ammeter is connected directly to the two ends of the battery. What happens?
am3.k: An ammeter has a very small resistance. Connecting it directly to the battery makes a short circuit: a huge current (tens of thousands of amperes) and a fire. In the simulation you can see this problem safely.
o: A huge current (short circuit) causes a fire and damages the devices.

tin9-phap-li-dich-vu-internet.reading:
Read part b) (textbook pages 18–19).
  • In 2006, the National Assembly passed the Law on Information Technology No. 67/2006/QH11.
  • In 2013, the Government issued Decree No. 72/2013/NĐ-CP on managing, providing and using Internet services and online information.
  • In 2018, the National Assembly passed the Law on Cybersecurity.
Internet users must avoid illegal actions against: national security, order and social safety; the personal rights and reputation of people and organisations; intellectual property, property, gambling; information security; illegal advertising; distorting history, harming national unity, insulting or discriminating.

vb.label: Reading – Legal documents
vb.q: Read part b). Match each legal document with its main content.
vb.k: 1 – a, 2 – b, 3 – c. All three documents list the banned actions.
items: 1) Law on Information Technology No. 67/2006/QH11 (2006)
2) Decree No. 72/2013/NĐ-CP (2013)
3) Law on Cybersecurity (2018)
opts: a) Rights and duties of organisations and people who use and develop IT
b) Managing, providing and using Internet services, online information and online games
c) Protecting national security, order and social safety in cyberspace

nhom.label: Reading – Groups of actions to avoid
nhom.q: Which group of illegal actions does each action belong to?
nhom.k: 1 – a, 2 – b, 3 – c, 4 – d, 5 – e. There is also the group distorting history, harming national unity, insulting, discriminating.

2) Posting another person's photo and number plate without permission
3) Sharing someone else's program code without permission
4) Spreading a virus through a fake prize link
5) Advertising weapons or selling rare animals

b) Personal rights and reputation of people and organisations
e) Illegal advertising of products and services

tin9-tim-hieu-phan-mem-mo-phong.reading: Read part 2 (textbook pages 21–22). Simulation software lets users learn about and study an object at low cost; study theory in a visual, lively way; create many situations to practise; and avoid situations that can damage equipment or be dangerous. But the quality of simulation software is not the same.

li.label: Reading – Benefits
li.q: Read part 2 (textbook pages 21–22). Which are benefits of simulation software?
li.k: The first four are benefits. Simulation software supports but does not fully replace real practice; the quality differs, so choose good software.
items: Learn about and study an object at low cost
Study theory in a visual, lively way by interacting
Create many situations to practise and study more fully
Avoid situations that damage equipment or are dangerous
Fully replace all real practice lessons
All simulation software is equally accurate

bq.label: Reading – Notes

tin9-trao-doi-hop-tac.tag: Reading Ways to use mind maps and presentations
tin9-trao-doi-hop-tac.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 27–28).
  • Present in person: easy to explain the big picture and the details, and to answer the audience's questions at once.
  • Share for others to view: when you cannot present in person; use pictures, charts and videos; keep a mind map on one page and attach files for details.
  • Share for members to update: each member edits at a time that suits them.
  • Share to work together in real time: everyone edits online at the same time; also open a chat channel to talk.
To use pictures, charts and videos well: use the right visual tool (simple, clear, gives the message best) and keep good quality (easy to see from far away, sharp, well arranged).

cach.label: Reading – Ways to use them
cach.q: Read part 1 (textbook pages 27–28). Which way of using a mind map or presentation is each situation?
cach.k: 1 – a, 2 – b, 3 – c, 4 – d. Presenting in person explains the big picture and answers questions at once; sharing lets people view, update and work together without meeting.
items: 1) The group leader presents the mind map to the class and answers questions at once
2) Sending the mind map file (with photos and videos) for the teacher to view later
3) Each member opens the online presentation and updates their part when it suits them
4) The whole group edits the online presentation together and talks in a chat channel
opts: b) Share for others to view
c) Share for members to update
d) Share to work together in real time

tq.label: Reading – Visual tools
tq.q: When you use pictures, charts and videos in a mind map or presentation, what should you do and what should you not do?
tq.k: Use the right visual tool (simple, clear, gives the message best) and keep good quality (easy to see from far away, sharp, well arranged, colours that attract attention).
items: Show a history with a timeline
Choose sharp pictures, well arranged and clear from far away
Use colours to attract attention
Add lots of pictures and effects even if they are not about the content
Use very small text and blurry pictures
Choose the most complicated visual possible
